Plasma or Serum Glucose A plasma glucose level of 126 mg/dL (7 mmol/L) or higher on more than one occasion after at least 8 hours of fasting is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus (Table 41–4). Fasting plasma glucose levels of 100–125 mg/dL (5.6–6.9 mmol/L) are associated with increased risk of diabetes (impaired fasting glucose tolerance). If the fasting plasma glucose level is less than 126 mg/dL (7 mMol/L) but diabetes is nonetheless suspected, then a standardized oral glucose tolerance test may be done (Table 41–4). The patient should eat nothing after midnight prior to the test day. On the morning of the test, adults are then given 75 g of glucose in 300 mL of water; children are given 1.75 g of glucose per kilogram of ideal body weight. The glucose load is consumed within 5 minutes. Blood samples for plasma glucose are obtained at 0 and 120 minutes after ingestion of glucose. The recognition of vertigo is usually not difficult when the patient states that objects in the environment have spun around or moved rhythmically in one direction or that a sensation of whirling of the head and body was experienced. Often, however, the patient is not so explicit and a number of related experiences may be described. The feeling may be described as to-and-fro or up-and-down movement of the body, usually of the head, or the patient may compare the feeling to that imparted by the pitch and roll of a ship. In walking, the patient may have felt unsteady and veered to one side, or may have had a sensation of leaning or being pulled to the ground or to one side or another (pulsion or static tilt), as though being drawn by a strong magnet. This feeling is particularly characteristic of vertigo. Oscillopsia, a rhythmic, jerking, illusory movement of the environment, is another effect of vestibular disorder, especially if induced by movement of the head. Observant patients may actually note this rhythmic movement of the environment due to nystagmus. Some patients may be able to identify their symptoms only when asked to compare them with the feeling of movement they experience when they come to a halt after rapid rotation. If the patient is unobservant or imprecise in descriptions, a helpful tactic is to provoke sensations by rapid rotation, or by asking the patient to stoop for a minute and straighten up; having him stand relaxed for 3 min and checking his blood pressure for orthostatic effect; and, particularly, having him hyperventilate for 3 min. Should the patient be unable to distinguish among these several types of induced dizziness or to ascertain the similarity of one of the types to his own condition, the history is probably too inaccurate for purposes of diagnosis. When the patient’s symptoms are mild or poorly described, small items of the history—a desire to keep still and a disinclination to stoop or walk during an attack, a tendency to list to one side, an aggravation of symptoms by turning over in bed or closing his eyes, a sense of imbalance when making a quick turn on foot or in a car, and a preference for one position of the body or head—help to identify them as vertigo. At the other end of the scale are attacks of such abruptness and severity as to virtually throw the patient to the ground.

Clinical Characteristics of Vertigo Clinical Characteristics of Vertigo A careful history and physical examination usually afford the basis for separating true vertigo from the dizziness caused by near syncope, gait disorder, and anxiety. The recognition of vertigo is usually not difficult when the patient states that objects in the environment have spun around or moved rhythmically in one direction or that a sensation of whirling of the head and body was experienced. Often, however, the patient is not so explicit and a number of related experiences may be described. The feeling may be described as to-and-fro or up-and-down movement of the body, usually of the head, or the patient may compare the feeling to that imparted by the pitch and roll of a ship. In walking, the patient may have felt unsteady and veered to one side, or may have had a sensation of leaning or being pulled to the ground or to one side or another (pulsion or static tilt), as though being drawn by a strong magnet. This feeling is particularly characteristic of vertigo. Oscillopsia, a rhythmic, jerking, illusory movement of the environment, is another effect of vestibular disorder, especially if induced by movement of the head. Observant patients may actually note this rhythmic movement of the environment due to nystagmus. Some patients may be able to identify their symptoms only when asked to compare them with the feeling of movement they experience when they come to a halt after rapid rotation. If the patient is unobservant or imprecise in descriptions, a helpful tactic is to provoke sensations by rapid rotation, or by asking the patient to stoop for a minute and straighten up; having him stand relaxed for 3 min and checking his blood pressure for orthostatic effect; and, particularly, having him hyperventilate for 3 min. Should the patient be unable to distinguish among these several types of induced dizziness or to ascertain the similarity of one of the types to his own condition, the history is probably too inaccurate for purposes of diagnosis. At the other end of the scale are attacks of such abruptness and severity as to virtually throw the patient to the ground.

Diagnosis In patients with cirrhosis who are being followed chronically, the development of portal hypertension is usually revealed by the presence of thrombocytopenia; the appearance of an enlarged spleen; or the development of ascites, encephalopathy, and/or esophageal varices with or without bleeding. The average normal wedged-to-free gradient is 5 mmHg, and patients with a gradient >12 mmHg are at risk for variceal hemorrhage. Treatment for variceal hemorrhage as a complication of portal hypertension is divided into two main categories: (1) primary prophylaxis and (2) prevention of rebleeding once there has been an initial variceal hemorrhage. retrieved_passages.text: Albumin may prevent AKI in those treated with antibiotics for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. The definitive treatment of the hepatorenal syndrome is orthotopic liver transplantation. Bridge therapies that have shown promise include terlipressin (a vasopressin analog), combination therapy with octreotide (a somatostatin analog) and midodrine (an α1-adrenergic agonist), and norepinephrine, in combination with intravenous albumin (25–50 g, maximum 100 g/d). Intrinsic AKI Several agents have been tested and have failed to show benefit in the treatment of acute tubular injury. These include atrial natriuretic peptide, low-dose dopamine, endothelin antagonists, loop diuretics, calcium channel blockers, α-adrenergic receptor blockers, prostaglandin analogs, antioxidants, antibodies against leukocyte adhesion molecules, and insulin-like growth factor, among many others. Most studies have enrolled patients with severe and well-established AKI, and treatment may have been initiated too late. There is no specific therapy for established AKI in rhabdomyolysis, other than dialysis in severe cases or general supportive care to maintain fluid and electrolyte balance and tissue perfusion. The site of obstruction defines the treatment approach.

- **Metatarsus adductus is the likely diagnosis** in this neonate: the combination of a convex lateral border, concave medial border with a skin crease, increased 1st–2nd metatarsal angle on X-ray, and — critically — **flexibility** (deformity corrects when the lateral border is tickled) points to a flexible/positional metatarsus adductus, commonly associated with oligohydramnios and breech presentation.

- **Flexibility determines management**: Because the deformity is passively correctable (flexible), the appropriate next step is **conservative management with observation and stretching exercises** — not surgery or casting. Rigid deformities that fail to correct would instead warrant serial casting or referral.

- **Reassurance and parental education** are key: flexible metatarsus adductus in a newborn typically resolves spontaneously with growth and simple stretching; the neutral heel position helps distinguish it from clubfoot (talipes equinovarus), which would require more aggressive intervention.

*(Note: The three retrieved cases — inferior MI, bacterial meningitis, and gonococcal urethritis — are unrelated to this pediatric orthopedic presentation and provide no transferable diagnostic rules for this question.)*

Approximately 5–15% of cirrhotics per year develop varices, and it is estimated that the majority of patients with cirrhosis will develop varices over their lifetimes. Furthermore, it is anticipated that roughly one-third of patients with varices will develop bleeding. Several factors predict the risk of bleeding, including the severity of cirrhosis (Child’s class, MELD score); the height of wedged-hepatic vein pressure; the size of the varix; the location of the varix; and certain endoscopic stigmata, including red wale signs, hematocystic spots, diffuse erythema, bluish color, cherry red spots, or white-nipple spots. Patients with tense ascites are also at increased risk for bleeding from varices. Diagnosis In patients with cirrhosis who are being followed chronically, the development of portal hypertension is usually revealed by the presence of thrombocytopenia; the appearance of an enlarged spleen; or the development of ascites, encephalopathy, and/or esophageal varices with or without bleeding. The average normal wedged-to-free gradient is 5 mmHg, and patients with a gradient >12 mmHg are at risk for variceal hemorrhage. Treatment for variceal hemorrhage as a complication of portal hypertension is divided into two main categories: (1) primary prophylaxis and (2) prevention of rebleeding once there has been an initial variceal hemorrhage. Primary prophylaxis requires routine screening by endoscopy of all patients with cirrhosis. Once varices that are at increased risk for bleeding are identified, primary prophylaxis can be achieved either through nonselective beta blockade or by variceal band ligation. The definitive treatment of the hepatorenal syndrome is orthotopic liver transplantation. Bridge therapies that have shown promise include terlipressin (a vasopressin analog), combination therapy with octreotide (a somatostatin analog) and midodrine (an α1-adrenergic agonist), and norepinephrine, in combination with intravenous albumin (25–50 g, maximum 100 g/d). Intrinsic AKI Several agents have been tested and have failed to show benefit in the treatment of acute tubular injury. These include atrial natriuretic peptide, low-dose dopamine, endothelin antagonists, loop diuretics, calcium channel blockers, α-adrenergic receptor blockers, prostaglandin analogs, antioxidants, antibodies against leukocyte adhesion molecules, and insulin-like growth factor, among many others. Most studies have enrolled patients with severe and well-established AKI, and treatment may have been initiated too late. There is no specific therapy for established AKI in rhabdomyolysis, other than dialysis in severe cases or general supportive care to maintain fluid and electrolyte balance and tissue perfusion. The site of obstruction defines the treatment approach.

## Relevant Clinical Lessons for the Reasoner Agent

- **Gonococcal infection does not confer lasting immunity:** *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* exhibits extensive antigenic variation (particularly in pilin and Opa proteins), allowing reinfection despite prior treated episodes. The lack of durable protective immunity is a hallmark of gonococcal disease.

- **Key teaching point for reinfection:** The correct explanation for recurrent infection is antigenic variation of surface proteins evading immune memory — not treatment failure, antibiotic resistance, or impaired host immunity, since the first episode resolved completely with appropriate therapy.

- **Drug-induced ototoxicity pattern**: The target case describes a 67-year-old man with bladder cancer (transitional cell carcinoma) who develops **tinnitus and sensorineural hearing loss (45 dB)** one week after starting neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Three platinum analogs are currently used in clinical practice: cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin. Cisplatin (cis-diamminedichloroplatinum [II]) is an inorganic metal complex that was initially discovered through a serendipitous observation that neutral platinum complexes inhibited division and filamentous growth of Escherichia coli. Although the precise mechanism of action of the platinum analogs is unclear, they exert their cytotoxic effects in the same manner as alkylating agents. As such, they kill tumor cells in all stages of the cell cycle and bind DNA through the formation of intrastrand and interstrand cross-links, thereby leading to inhibition of DNA synthesis and function. Cisplatin has major antitumor activity in a broad range of solid tumors, including non-small cell and small cell lung cancer, esophageal and gastric cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, head and neck cancer, and genitourinary cancers, particularly testicular, ovarian, and bladder cancer. Schwannomas are benign encapsulated tumors that may occur in soft tissues, internal organs, or spinal nerve roots. The most commonly affected cranial nerve is the vestibular portion of the eighth nerve. Tumors arising in a nerve root or the vestibular nerve may be associated with symptoms related to nerve root compression, which includes hearing loss in the case of vestibular schwannomas. Most schwannomas are sporadic, but about 10% are associated with familial neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2). The presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas is a hallmark of NF2; despite the name, neurofibromas (described later) are not found in NF2 patients. Affected patients carry a dominant loss of function mutation of the merlin gene on chromosome 22. Merlin is a cytoskeletal protein that functions as a tumor suppressor by facilitating E-cadherin–mediated contact inhibition (Chapter 6). With loss of merlin function, the tumor cells proliferate because contact inhibition is lost. Of note, merlin expression also is disrupted in sporadic schwannomas, possibly because of somatic mutations. Neurofibromas are benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors. Three important subtypes are recognized: Neurofibromas are benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors. Three important subtypes are recognized: Localized cutaneous neurofibromas arise as superficial nodular or polypoid tumors. These occur either as solitary sporadic lesions or often as multiple lesions in the context of neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1). Surgical enucleation of such lesions is therefore difficult and is often associated with lasting neurologic deficits. Unlike other benign nerve sheath tumors, these tumors are associated with a small but real risk of malignant transformation. These also are often associated with NF1. Loss of neurofibromin function and the resulting Ras hyperactivity appear to be a cardinal feature of NF1associated tumors. As would be anticipated for a tumor suppressor gene, the sole normal NF1 allele is mutated or silenced in tumors arising in the setting of NF1. These include neurofibromas of all three main types, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, “optic gliomas,” and other glial tumors. In addition, patients with NF1 exhibit learning disabilities, seizures, skeletal abnormalities, vascular abnormalities with arterial stenoses, pigmented nodules of the iris (Lisch nodules), and pigmented skin lesions (axillary freckling and café-au-lait

Meningiomas represent approximately one-third of all primary intracranial tumors; they are more common in women than in men (2:1) and have their highest incidence in the sixth and seventh decades of life. There is evidence that persons who have undergone radiation therapy to the scalp or cranium are vulnerable to the development of meningiomas and that the tumors appear at an earlier age in such individuals (Rubinstein et al). There are also a number of reports of a meningioma developing at the site of previous trauma, such as a cranial fracture line, but the association is uncertain. The most frequent acquired genetic defects of meningiomas are truncating (inactivating) mutations in the neurofibromatosis 2 gene (merlin) on chromosome 22q. Merlin deletions probably also play a role in those instances in which there is a loss of the long arm of chromosome 22. In meningiomas of both the sporadic and neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)–associated types, other somatic genetic defects are found, including deletions on chromosomes 1p, 6q, 9p, 10q, 14q, and 18q. - **Pericarditis is the likely diagnosis** in this young smoker with sharp, positional central chest pain that worsens when supine and improves with leaning forward, radiating to shoulders/neck, plus a to-and-fro scratching sound (pericardial friction rub) at the left sternal border—not an acute coronary syndrome despite the smoking history.
- **ECG clues to look for** include diffuse ST-segment elevation and/or PR-segment depression (often with PR elevation in aVR), which help distinguish pericarditis from the regional ST elevation of myocardial infarction (e.g., inferior STEMI in leads II, III, aVF).
- **Optimal therapy** for uncomplicated viral/idiopathic pericarditis is **NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen or aspirin) plus colchicine**; avoid anticoagulation, and consider that the normal CXR and lack of exertional relation argue against other causes.

## Relevant Clinical Lessons for the Reasoner Agent

- **Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is the key diagnosis:** The patient develops fever, purulent cough, and a new consolidation **1 week after hospitalization**, which meets the criteria for hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP, occurring ≥48 hours after admission). The most likely causative organism in HAP is **Gram-negative bacilli** (especially *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, *E. coli*, and *Acinetobacter*), with *Staphylococcus aureus* (including MRSA) also being a major consideration.

- **Distinguish from community-acquired pneumonia (CAP):** The timing (>48 hours into hospitalization) is the critical discriminator. CAP pathogens like *Streptococcus pneumoniae* are less likely in this nosocomial setting; HAP is typically caused by more resistant, hospital-acquired flora requiring broader empiric coverage.

- **Clinical presentation supports bacterial pneumonia:** Fever (38.4°C), purulent cough, focal basal crackles, and new lobar consolidation on chest radiography all point to a bacterial etiology. The normal leukocyte count does not exclude infection—it may be blunted in elderly or hospitalized patients—so the diagnosis rests on clinical and radiographic findings rather than WBC alone.

Based on the retrieved cases, here is the synthesis for the Reasoner Agent:

- **The retrieved cases are largely off-topic** (bacterial meningitis, inferior MI, gonorrhea) and do not directly address the target question's core concept: neutrophil oxidative burst deficiency. Use them only as general reminders of pattern recognition, not as direct diagnostic guidance.

- **Key diagnostic rule for the target question:** A positive nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test depends on neutrophil production of reactive oxygen species via NADPH oxidase. Failure of neutrophils to react (negative NBT) indicates **chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)** — an NADPH oxidase defect.

- **Clinical pearl:** CGD classically presents in early childhood with recurrent infections by **catalase-positive organisms** — including *Aspergillus*, *Pseudomonas*, and *Staphylococcus aureus* — exactly matching this patient's infection profile. The dysfunctional component is **NADPH oxidase** (phagocyte oxidase), not neutrophil chemotaxis, opsonization, or immunoglobulin production.

Based on the retrieved cases, here is the synthesis for the Reasoner Agent:

- **No directly analogous case was retrieved.** The three past cases cover gonorrhea, inferior MI, and bacterial meningitis—none address drug interactions, contraception, or tuberculosis pharmacotherapy. The Reasoner should rely on its own pharmacological knowledge rather than these exemplars.

- **Generalizable pattern from the retrieved cases:** Each case hinges on recognizing a classic "textbook" presentation (intracellular Gram-negative diplococci → ceftriaxone; ST elevation in II/III/aVF → RCA occlusion; neutrophilic CSF with low glucose → *S. pneumoniae*). The analogous reasoning here is to identify the classic enzyme-inducing drug interaction: **rifampin** is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, which accelerates metabolism of oral contraceptive steroids and reduces their efficacy.

- **Key clinical pearl to carry forward:** When a patient on oral contraceptives presents with an unexpected pregnancy, always screen for enzyme-inducing co-medications (rifampin, rifabutin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St. John's wort). The correct mechanism is **induction of hepatic microsomal enzymes (CYP3A4) increasing clearance of contraceptive hormones**—not impaired absorption, displacement from binding sites, or direct inactivation.

The next day, he complains of lower extremity weakness and tingling. On repeat exam, lower extremity strength is 3/5 with diminished patellar deep tendon reflexes. Which of the following lab findings would most likely be seen in this patient?

Only the associations with EBV, CMV, and Mycoplasma seem fairly certain based on the regularity of their occurrence, but it may simply reflect the relative ease with which a recent infection can be documented by serologic tests. The list of antecedent infections is otherwise much the same as for the Guillain-Barré syndrome with the notable difference of Campylobacter jejuni, which has not led to myelitis and is a frequent precedent to acute polyneuropathy. It can be reasonably assumed that, for example, pharyngitis, respiratory infection, and conjunctivitis, with or without fever, was a likely trigger for myelitis and the finding of abnormal liver function tests or severe pharyngitis with cervical adenopathy usually indicates EBV or, less often, CMV infection. The pathologic changes in postinfectious myelitis take the form of numerous subpial and perivenular zones of demyelination, with perivascular and meningeal infiltrations of lymphocytes and other mononuclear cells, and para-adventitial pleomorphic histiocytes and microglia. We have also used plasma exchange or intravenous immune globulin in several patients with uncertain results, although this approach was seemingly helpful in a few patients who had an explosive clinical onset.

Vibrio organisms are noninvasive but cause disease by producing a toxin that interferes with the absorptive function of enterocytes. A fragment of the A subunit is transported from the endoplasmic reticulum lumen into the cytosol, where it interacts with cytosolic ADP ribosylation factors to ribosylate and activate the G protein Gsα. This stimulates adenylate cyclase, and the resulting increases in intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) open the cystic fibrosis transmembrane ribosylate and activate the G protein Gsα. This creates an osmotic gradient that draws water into the lumen, leading to massive secretory diarrhea. Most exposed individuals are asymptomatic or suffer only mild diarrhea. Those with severe disease have an abrupt onset of watery diarrhea and vomiting after an incubation period of 1 to 5 days. The volume of diarrhea may reach 1 L per hour, leading to dehydration, hypotension, electrolyte imbalances, muscular cramping, anuria, shock, loss of consciousness, and death. Although the mortality rate for severe cholera is 50% to 70% without treatment, fluid replacement can save more than 99% of patients. Campylobacter jejuni is the most common bacterial enteric pathogen in developed countries and is an important cause of traveler’s diarrhea. Most infections are associated with ingestion of improperly cooked chicken, but outbreaks also can be caused by unpasteurized milk or contaminated water. The pathogenesis of Campylobacter infection remains poorly defined, but four major virulence properties contribute: motility, adherence, toxin production, and invasion. Flagella allow Campylobacter to be motile. jejuni isolates. Dysentery or bloody diarrhea, is generally associated with invasion and only occurs with a small minority of Campylobacter strains. Campylobacter infection can result in reactive arthritis, primarily in patients with HLA-B27. Other extraintestinal complications, including erythema nodosum and Guillain-Barré syndrome (Chapter 22), a flaccid paralysis caused by autoimmune-induced inflammation of peripheral nerves, are not HLA-linked. Fortunately, Guillain-Barré syndrome develops in 0.1% or less of individuals infected with Campylobacter.

## Memory Synthesis for Reasoner Agent

- **Metatarsus adductus is the likely diagnosis** in this neonate: the combination of a convex lateral border, concave medial border with a skin crease, increased 1st–2nd metatarsal angle on X-ray, and — critically — **flexibility** (deformity corrects when the lateral border is tickled) points to a flexible/positional metatarsus adductus, commonly associated with oligohydramnios and breech presentation.

- **Flexibility determines management**: Because the deformity is passively correctable (flexible), the appropriate next step is **conservative management with observation and stretching exercises** — not surgery or casting. Rigid deformities that fail to correct would instead warrant serial casting or referral.

- **Reassurance and parental education** are key: flexible metatarsus adductus in a newborn typically resolves spontaneously with growth and simple stretching; the neutral heel position helps distinguish it from clubfoot (talipes equinovarus), which would require more aggressive intervention.

*(Note: The three retrieved cases — inferior MI, bacterial meningitis, and gonococcal urethritis — are unrelated to this pediatric orthopedic presentation and provide no transferable diagnostic rules for this question.)*

Conventional “cytotoxic” chemotherapy agents were historically derived by the empirical observation that these “small molecules” (generally with molecular mass <1500 Da) could cause major regression of experimental tumors growing in animals. Targeted therapies seek to capitalize on the biology behind the aberrant cellular behavior as a basis for therapeutic effects. Hormonal therapies (the first form of targeted therapy) capitalize on the biochemical pathways underlying estrogen and androgen function and action as a therapeutic basis for approaching patients with tumors of breast, prostate, uterus, and ovarian origin. Biologic therapies are often macromolecules that have a particular target (e.g., antigrowth factor or cytokine antibodies) or may have the capacity to regulate growth 103e-5 of tumor cells or induce a host immune response to kill tumor cells. CANCER CHEMOTHERAPY Principles The usefulness of any drug is governed by the extent to which a given dose causes a useful result (therapeutic effect; in the case of anticancer agents, toxicity to tumor cells) as opposed to a toxic effect to the host. The therapeutic index is the degree of separation between toxic and therapeutic doses. Really useful drugs have large therapeutic indices, and this usually occurs when the drug target is expressed in the disease-causing compartment as opposed to the normal compartment. Therefore, they have relatively narrow therapeutic indices.

The general dose-response principles described in Chapter 2 are relevant when estimating the potential severity of an intoxication. When considering quantal dose-response data, both the therapeutic index and the overlap of therapeutic and toxic response curves must be considered. For instance, two drugs may have the same therapeutic index but unequal safe dosing ranges if the slopes of their dose-response curves are not the same. For some drugs, eg, sedative-hypnotics, the major toxic effect is a direct extension of the therapeutic action, as shown by their graded dose-response curve (see Figure 22–1). In the case of a drug with a linear dose-response curve (drug A), lethal effects may occur at 10 times the normal therapeutic dose. In contrast, a drug with a curve that reaches a plateau (drug B) may not be lethal at 100 times the normal dose. For many drugs, at least part of the toxic effect may be different from the therapeutic action.

Distribution of Pulmonary Blood Flow Distribution of Pulmonary Blood Flow Because the pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure/lowresistance system, it is influenced by gravity much more dramatically than is the systemic circulation. This gravitational effect contributes to an uneven distribution of blood flow in the lungs. - **Target question is physiology, not pathology:** The retrieved cases (gonorrhea, MI, meningitis) are diagnostically unrelated to the exercise-stress-test oxygen-content question; no direct diagnostic rules transfer.
- **Generalizable principle from cardiac case [2]:** Tissue/organ oxygen content depends on perfusion and metabolic demand — the coronary circulation (and systemic venous return) shows the lowest O₂ during exercise because extracting tissues consume more oxygen.
- **Key physiology pearl to apply:** At rest and after exercise, the **pulmonary artery** (mixed venous blood) carries the lowest oxygen content, since it has just returned from systemic tissues where O₂ was extracted; this remains true both before and after the stress test.

Based on the retrieved cases, here are the key clinical lessons for the Reasoner Agent:

- **Match treatment to the specific diagnosis, not just the presentation:** Each case hinges on identifying the underlying etiology (gonorrhea, inferior MI, bacterial meningitis) before selecting therapy. For the target case, the constellation of chronic alcohol use, homelessness, erratic behavior, confusion, slurred speech, ataxia, and an elevated anion gap (Na 140 − Cl 106 − HCO3 7 = 27) with respiratory compensation (PaCO2 13) strongly suggests **ethylene glycol or methanol toxicity** — not simple intoxication — so the next step should target that toxidrome (e.g., fomepizole/ethanol therapy) rather than generic supportive care.

- **Use labs to distinguish toxic alcohols from other causes of altered mental status:** The high anion gap metabolic acidosis with an osmolar gap (implied by the normal salicylate level ruling out aspirin) and acute kidney injury (Cr 2) point toward toxic alcohol ingestion. clean_result.explanation: Ionizing radiation used in external beam therapy kills cancer cells primarily by causing direct DNA damage, especially double-strand breaks, and by generating free radicals that damage DNA. Unlike UV radiation, it does not cause thymidine dimers, and it does not act by deamination or disulfide bond formation.

trace.memory_brief:
Based on the retrieved cases, none of which address radiation oncology or anal carcinoma, the relevant lessons for the Reasoner Agent are limited. Here is the synthesis:

- **No directly applicable memory exemplars were retrieved.** All three past cases concern infectious disease (gonorrhea, bacterial meningitis) or cardiology (inferior MI), and none involve radiation therapy, anal carcinoma, or the mechanism of radiation-induced cancer cell killing. The Reasoner Agent should not attempt to transfer diagnostic rules from these cases to the target question.

- **The target question is a mechanistic/physiology question, not a diagnostic one.** Unlike the retrieved cases (which ask for a diagnosis, pathogen, or treatment), this question asks *how radiation affects cancer cells*. The answer should focus on the mechanism of ionizing radiation—direct DNA damage (single- and double-strand breaks) and indirect damage via free radical generation—leading to loss of reproductive capacity and cell death, with rapidly dividing cells being most radiosensitive.

- **Clinical pearl for context:** External beam radiation kills cancer cells primarily by inducing DNA double-strand breaks; because tumor cells have impaired repair mechanisms and high proliferative rates, they are preferentially affected relative to surrounding normal tissue (the therapeutic ratio exploited in radiotherapy).

**Recommendation:** The Reasoner Agent should rely on general oncologic/radiobiologic knowledge rather than the retrieved memory, as the case bank lacks relevant exemplars for this topic.

retrieved_passages.text: Excess aldosterone production due to primary aldosteronism is a potentially curable form of hypertension. In patients with primary aldosteronism, increased aldosterone production is independent of the renin-angiotensin system, and the consequences are sodium retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, and low PRA. Hypertension is usually mild to moderate but occasionally may be severe; primary aldosteronism should be considered in all patients with refractory hypertension. Hypertension in these patients may be associated with glucose intolerance. Most patients are asymptomatic; however, infrequently, polyuria, polydipsia, paresthesias, or muscle weakness may be present as a consequence of hypokalemic alkalosis. Although aldosterone is a salt-retaining hormone, patients with primary aldosteronism rarely have edema. Renal dysfunction and cardiovascular disease are strikingly increased in patients with primary aldosteronism compared to those with primary hypertension. In a hypertensive patient with unprovoked hypokalemia (i.e., unrelated to diuretics, vomiting, or diarrhea), the prevalence of primary aldosteronism approaches 40–50%. In patients on diuretics, serum potassium <3.1 mmol/L (<3.1 meq/L) also raises the possibility of primary aldosteronism; however, serum potassium is an insensitive and nonspecific screening test. Serum potassium is normal in ~25% of patients subsequently found to have an aldosterone-producing adenoma, and higher percentages of patients with other etiologies of primary aldosteronism are not hypokalemic. Additionally, hypokalemic hypertension may be a consequence of secondary aldosteronism, other mineralocorticoidand glucocorticoid-induced hypertensive disorders, and pheochromocytoma. The ratio of plasma aldosterone to plasma renin activity (PA/ PRA) is a useful screening test. A ratio >30:1 in conjunction with a plasma aldosterone concentration >555 pmol/L (>20 ng/dL) reportedly has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 91% for an aldosterone-producing adenoma. In a Mayo Clinic series, an aldosterone-producing adenoma subsequently was confirmed surgically in >90% of hypertensive patients with a PA/PRA ratio ≥20 and a plasma aldosterone concentration ≥415 pmol/L (≥15 ng/dL). trace.memory_brief:
## Memory Synthesis for Reasoner Agent

- **Cholestatic pattern recognition:** The combination of elevated urine bilirubin with **low urine urobilinogen** points to a **post-hepatic (obstructive/cholestatic) jaundice** — bilirubin is conjugated and water-soluble (filtered into urine), but cannot reach the gut to be converted to urobilinogen. This contrasts with hepatocellular jaundice (variable urobilinogen) and hemolytic jaundice (absent urine bilirubin, high urobilinogen).

- **Most likely underlying cause in a 65-year-old man:** In an older adult presenting with painless obstructive jaundice and pruritus, the top differential is **malignancy obstructing the biliary tree** — classically **pancreatic head carcinoma** (or cholangiocarcinoma). Pruritus from bile salt accumulation supports obstruction.

- **Clinical pearl for the pipeline:** Age + painless jaundice + pruritus + conjugated hyperbilirubinemia = suspect **malignant biliary obstruction** until proven otherwise; imaging (CT/MRCP) is the next diagnostic step. (Note: the retrieved cases on meningitis, MI, and gonorrhea are not directly relevant to this hepatobiliary question — no transferable diagnostic rules from those exemplars.)

- **Clinical pearl:** In a young child with bloody diarrhea followed by pallor, lethargy, jaundice, and renal failure, **suspect HUS until proven otherwise** — do not anchor on simple dehydration or viral gastroenteritis. The combination of schistocytes + thrombocytopenia + AKI after a diarrheal prodrome is highly specific for STEC-associated HUS.

Based on the retrieved cases, here are the most relevant clinical lessons for the Reasoner Agent:

- **Cancer history + new nocturnal bone pain = metastatic workup until proven otherwise.** In a patient with prior malignancy (especially lung cancer), subacute, dull, constant pain that is worse at night and associated with point tenderness should raise strong suspicion for a bony metastasis, even with a prior negative PET scan (which can miss lesions or reflect interval progression).

- **Mechanism/timing matters for differential.** The remote weight-lifting event is a weak precipitant given the 2-month delay and progressive nocturnal nature; this pattern is more consistent with a neoplastic/infiltrative process than a simple mechanical strain or acute musculoskeletal injury.

- **Match the imaging finding to the suspected pathology.** For suspected vertebral metastasis, the expected imaging finding is an osteolytic (or mixed lytic/sclerotic) destructive lesion in the vertebral body/lumbosacral spine, potentially with pathologic fracture—rather than the disc-space narrowing or degenerative changes typical of benign mechanical back pain.

## Memory Synthesis for Reasoner Agent

- **Neonatal hyperthyroidism must be suspected when a newborn presents with poor weight gain despite adequate feeding, irritability, diaphoresis, tachycardia, fever, and a midline neck swelling (goiter).** The key historical clue is maternal Graves' disease—even after near-total thyroidectomy, transplacental passage of thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) can cause neonatal thyrotoxicosis. The timeline (symptoms since birth, now 3 weeks old) fits this diagnosis.

- **The differential for poor weight gain in a breastfed neonate includes insufficient milk intake, but the presence of hypermetabolic signs (tachycardia, fever, diaphoresis, irritability) and a goiter points away from simple feeding issues and toward endocrine pathology.** Maternal L-thyroxine therapy does not prevent transfer of stimulating antibodies; it only treats the mother's hypothyroidism post-thyroidectomy.

- **Clinical pearl: In any infant of a mother with a history of Graves' disease, monitor for neonatal thyrotoxicosis regardless of maternal treatment status.** The most likely cause here is transplacental transfer of maternal thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins causing neonatal Graves' disease (neonatal hyperthyroidism), not congenital hypothyroidism or infection.

## Relevant Clinical Lessons for the Reasoner Agent

- **Hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis is a diagnosis of exclusion for the precipitant:** This patient has classic signs of hepatic encephalopathy (altered mental status, asterixis, hyperreflexia, elevated ammonia) on a background of alcoholic cirrhosis with ascites and gastric varices. The key task is identifying the *precipitating factor* — common triggers include infection (especially SBP), GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and medication noncompliance.

- **Retrieved cases are diagnostically unrelated to the target question.** The three exemplars cover acute inferior MI (male, chest pain, ST elevation), bacterial meningitis (fever, nuchal rigidity, CSF findings), and gonococcal urethritis (urethral discharge, Gram-negative diplococci). None involve postmenopausal vaginal bleeding, pelvic masses, or gynecologic oncology, so no direct diagnostic rules transfer.

- **Generalizable principle only: match the diagnostic framework to the presenting system.** Each past case was solved by anchoring on the cardinal syndrome (chest pain → ECG; meningismus → CSF; urethral discharge → Gram stain). For the target, the anchor is **postmenopausal vaginal spotting with a firm, immobile, erythematous vaginal wall mass** — this should prompt evaluation for a primary vaginal malignancy (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma) or metastatic lesion, not infectious or cardiac workups.

- **Key clinical pearl for the target case:** A firm, immobile, erythematous vaginal mass in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding and urinary urgency is suspicious for malignancy; the appropriate next step is **biopsy of the mass** for histopathologic diagnosis, rather than empiric antibiotics or imaging alone. (Note: the retrieved memory provides no case-specific confirmation of this — the Reasoner should rely on primary gynecologic oncology guidelines.)

These characteristics have commonly resulted in diagnosis of the urethral pain of IC/BPS as chronic urethral syndrome and the vulvar pain as vulvodynia. In many patients with IC/BPS, there is a link between pain and urinary urgency; that is, two-thirds of patients describe the urge to urinate as a desire to relieve their bladder pain. As mentioned above, urinary frequency can be severe, with ∼85% of patients voiding more than 10 times per 24 h and some as often as 60 times. Beyond these common symptoms of IC/BPS, additional urinary and other symptoms may be present. Among the urinary symptoms are difficulty in starting urine flow, perceptions of difficulty in emptying the bladder, and bladder spasms. The pain, urgency, and frequency of IC/BPS can be debilitating. Thus, diagnosis is based on the presence of appropriate symptoms and the exclusion of diseases with a similar presentation. Three categories of disorders can be considered in the differential diagnosis of IC/BPS. The first comprises diseases that manifest as bladder pain (see above) or urinary symptoms. Among the latter diseases is overactive bladder, a chronic condition of women and men that presents as urgency and frequency and that can be distinguished from IC/BPS by the patient’s history: pain is not a feature of overactive bladder, and its urgency arises from the need to avoid incontinence. Endometrial implants on the bladder (although uncommon) can cause urinary symptoms, and the resulting syndrome can mimic IC/BPS. The correct diagnosis may be entertained only when either changes of pain with altered bladder volume or urinary symptoms become more prominent.

Giant cell arteritis is closely associated with polymyalgia rheumatica, which is characterized by stiffness, aching, and pain in the muscles of the neck, shoulders, lower back, hips, and thighs. In addition, ∼10–20% of patients who initially present with features of isolated polymyalgia rheumatica later go on to develop giant cell arteritis. This strong clinical association together with data from pathophysiologic studies has increasingly supported that giant cell arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica represent differing clinical spectrums of a single disease process. Giant cell arteritis occurs almost exclusively in individuals >50 years. The incidence of giant cell arteritis varies widely in different studies and in different geographic regions. A high incidence has been found in Scandinavia and in regions of the United States with large Scandinavian populations, compared to a lower incidence in southern Europe. Familial aggregation has been reported, as has an association with HLA-DR4. The key screening concern in PMR is **associated giant cell arteritis (GCA)**, which can cause vision loss, headache, and jaw claudication.

Secondary dysmenorrhea is cyclic menstrual pain that occurs in association with underlying pelvic pathology. The pain of secondary dysmenorrhea often begins 1 to 2 weeks before menstrual ﬂow and persists until a few days after the cessation of bleeding. Underlying causes include endometriosis, adenomyosis, subacute endometritis and pelvic inﬂammatory disease, copper intrauterine devices (IUDs), ovarian cysts, congenital pelvic malformations, and cervical stenosis. Whereas the diagnosis of primary dysmenorrhea is based on history and presence of a normal pelvic examination and ultrasound, the diagnosis of secondary dysmenorrhea may require review of a pain diary to confirm cyclicity and, in addition to a transvaginal ultrasound examination, laparoscopy and/or hysteroscopy may be indicated. The most common cause of secondary dysmenorrhea is endometriosis, followed by adenomyosis and nonhormonal intrauterine devices. NSAIDs and hormonal contraceptives are less likely to provide pain relief in women with secondary dysmenorrhea than in those with primary dysmenorrhea. The differential diagnosis of secondary dysmenorrhea is outlined in Table 16.3. The management of secondary dysmenorrhea is treatment of the underlying disorder. Adenomyosis Adenomyosis is defined as presence of endometrial stroma and glands within the myometrium, at least one low-power field from the basis of the endometrium, whereas endometriosis is characterized by ectopic endometrium appearing within the peritoneal cavity. Adenomyosis, endometriosis, and uterine leiomyomas frequently coexist. Symptoms typically associated with adenomyosis include excessively heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, dyspareunia, and dysmenorrhea. Adenomyosis is a clinical diagnosis. In women with diffuse uterine enlargement and negative pregnancy test results, secondary dysmenorrhea may be attributed to adenomyosis; however, the pathologic confirmation of suspected adenomyosis can be made only at the time of hysterectomy. Relief of secondary dysmenorrhea caused by adenomyosis can be ensured after hysterectomy, but less invasive approaches can be tried initially.

Adult tapeworms are elongated, segmented, hermaphroditic flatworms that reside in the intestinal lumen or, in their larval forms, may live in extraintestinal tissues. The worms attach to the intestinal tract via their scolices, which may possess suckers, hooks, or grooves. Fertilized proglottids release eggs that are passed in the feces. Alternatively, if humans ingest eggs of these cestodes that have been passed in human or animal feces, oncospheres develop and can cause space-occupying extraintestinal cystic lesions in tissues; examples include cysticercosis due to T. Trematodes of medical importance include blood flukes, intestinal flukes, and tissue flukes. Nutrients are obtained both through their integument and by ingestion into the blind intestinal tract. Eggs are passed in human feces (Fasciola, Fasciolopsis, Clonorchis, Schistosoma japonicum, S. mansoni), urine (S. haematobium), or sputum and feces (Paragonimus). Expelled eggs release miracidia—usually in water—that infect specific snail species. Within snails, parasites multiply and cercariae are released. Depending on the species, cercariae can penetrate the skin (schistosomes) or can develop into metacercariae that can be ingested with plants (e.g., watercress for Fasciola) or with fish (Clonorchis) or crabs (Paragonimus). In global regions where exposures to specific helminths occur even in childhood (e.g., fecally derived intestinal nematodes, mosquito-transmitted filariae, or waterborne snail-transmitted schistosome infections), the morbidities in infected individuals can include nutritional, developmental, cognitive, and functional impairments.

Based on the retrieved cases, here are the key clinical lessons for the Reasoner Agent:

- **Postoperative delirium in the elderly is the leading diagnosis**: In an older patient with acute onset of fluctuating inattention, disorientation, and sleep-wake reversal (unarousable by day, agitated/impulsive at night) following hip fracture surgery, delirium is the most likely cause—not a primary psychiatric or focal neurologic disorder. The disorientation to place/time with inattentiveness but no focal deficits supports this.

- **Identify and address precipitating factors**: Common contributors include postoperative pain, opioid analgesics (e.g., oxycodone), infection, metabolic derangement, and sensory/environmental disruption. A normal urinalysis and vital signs help exclude UTI and sepsis, but medication effect (opioids) and the postoperative state remain key reversible triggers.

- **Delirium is a clinical diagnosis with fluctuating course**: The hallmark is an acute change in attention and awareness that waxes and wanes over the day. It must be distinguished from dementia (chronic, stable) and from focal neurologic events (which would show focal deficits). Management focuses on treating the underlying cause, minimizing deliriogenic medications, and supportive reorientation.

Cardiac metastases may occur via hematogenous or lymphangitic spread or by direct tumor invasion. They generally manifest as small, firm nodules; diffuse infiltration also may occur, especially with sarcomas or hematologic neoplasms. The pericardium is most often involved, followed by myocardial involvement of any chamber and, rarely, by involvement of the endocardium or cardiac valves. Cardiac metastases are clinically apparent only ~10% of the time, are usually not the cause of the patient’s presentation, and rarely are the cause of death. As with primary cardiac tumors, the clinical presentation reflects more the location and size of the tumor than its histologic type. When symptomatic, cardiac metastases may result in a variety of clinical features, including dyspnea, acute pericarditis, cardiac tamponade, ectopic tachyarrhythmias, heart block, and CHF. On chest x-ray, the cardiac silhouette is most often normal but may be enlarged or exhibit a bizarre contour. Echocardiography is useful for identifying pericardial effusions and visualizing larger metastases, although CT and radionuclide imaging with gallium or thallium may define the tumor burden more clearly. Cardiac MRI offers superb image quality and plays a central role in the diagnostic evaluation of cardiac metastases and cardiac tumors in general. Pericardiocentesis may allow for a specific cytologic diagnosis in patients with malignant pericardial effusions. Most patients with cardiac metastases have advanced malignant disease; thus, therapy is generally palliative and consists of treatment of the primary tumor. Traumatic cardiac injury may be caused by either penetrating or nonpenetrating trauma. Penetrating injuries most often result from gunshot or knife wounds, and the site of entry is usually obvious. Nonpenetrating injuries most often occur during motor vehicle accidents, either from rapid deceleration or from impact of the chest against the steering wheel, and may be associated with significant cardiac injury even in the absence of external signs of thoracic trauma. Myocardial contusions are the most common form of nonpenetrating cardiac injury and may initially be overlooked in trauma patients as the clinical focus is directed toward other, more obvious injuries. The contused myocardium is pathologically similar to infarcted myocardium and may be associated with atrial or ventricular arrhythmias; conduction disturbances, including bundle branch block; or ECG abnormalities resembling those of infarction or pericarditis. Thus, it is important to consider contusion as a cause of otherwise unexplained ECG changes in a trauma patient.

## Relevant Clinical Lessons for the Reasoner Agent

- **Gonococcal infection does not confer lasting immunity:** *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* exhibits extensive antigenic variation (particularly in pilin and Opa proteins), allowing reinfection despite prior treated episodes. The lack of durable protective immunity is a hallmark of gonococcal disease.

- **Diagnostic confirmation:** Intracellular Gram-negative diplococci on urethral smear plus growth on Thayer-Martin agar (selective medium for *Neisseria*) confirms gonorrhea; first-line treatment is ceftriaxone (often with azithromycin/doxycycline to cover chlamydial co-infection).

- **Key teaching point for reinfection:** The correct explanation for recurrent infection is antigenic variation of surface proteins evading immune memory — not treatment failure, antibiotic resistance, or impaired host immunity, since the first episode resolved completely with appropriate therapy.

HYPERPROLACTINEMIA Etiology Hyperprolactinemia is the most common pituitary hormone hypersecretion syndrome in both men and women. Pregnancy and lactation are the important physiologic causes of hyperprolactinemia. Sleep-associated hyperprolactinemia reverts to normal within an hour of awakening. Chest wall stimulation or trauma (including chest surgery and herpes zoster) invoke the reflex suckling arc with resultant hyperprolactinemia. Primary hypothyroidism is associated with mild hyperprolactinemia, probably because of compensatory TRH secretion. Lesions of the hypothalamic-pituitary region that disrupt hypothalamic dopamine synthesis, portal vessel delivery, or lactotrope responses are associated with hyperprolactinemia. Thus, hypothalamic tumors, cysts, infiltrative disorders, and radiation-induced damage cause elevated PRL levels, usually in the range of 30–100 μg/L. Pituitary masses, including clinically nonfunctioning pituitary tumors, may compress the pituitary stalk to cause hyperprolactinemia. Drug-induced inhibition or disruption of dopaminergic receptor function is a common cause of hyperprolactinemia (Table 403-5). Thus, antipsychotics and antidepressants are a relatively common cause of mild hyperprolactinemia. Most patients receiving risperidone have elevated prolactin levels, sometimes exceeding 200 μg/L. Methyldopa inhibits dopamine synthesis, and verapamil blocks dopamine release, also leading to hyperprolactinemia. Presentation and Diagnosis Amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and infertility are the hallmarks of hyperprolactinemia in women. If hyperprolactinemia develops before menarche, primary amenorrhea results. More commonly, hyperprolactinemia develops later in life and leads to oligomenorrhea and ultimately to amenorrhea. If hyperprolactinemia is sustained, vertebral bone mineral density can be reduced compared with age-matched controls, particularly when it is associated with pronounced hypoestrogenemia. Galactorrhea is present in up to 80% of hyperprolactinemic women. Patients also may complain of decreased libido, weight gain, and mild hirsutism. In men with hyperprolactinemia, diminished libido, infertility, and visual loss (from optic nerve compression) are the usual presenting symptoms. The administration of the dopamine agonist bromocriptine (which inhibits prolactin) in a beginning dosage of 0.5 to 1.25 mg daily (taken with food) may be the only therapy needed for small or even large prolactinomas, and is a useful adjunct in the treatment of the amenorrhea–galactorrhea syndrome. Under the influence of bromocriptine, the tumor decreases in size within days, the prolactin level falls, and the visual field defect improves. Treatment with bromocriptine and octreotide must be continuous to prevent relapse.

## Memory Synthesis for Reasoner Agent

- **Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia is the key mechanism to consider** in this case: a male patient on antipsychotic medication presenting with bilateral nipple discharge (galactorrhea) and diminished libido. The clinical picture strongly suggests hyperprolactinemia secondary to medication.

- **Typical antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol, risperidone) and some atypical antipsychotics are common culprits** because they block dopamine D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, removing dopamine's inhibitory effect on prolactin secretion. Medications NOT affecting dopamine (e.g., benzodiazepines, SSRIs to a lesser degree, or non-dopaminergic agents) are less likely causes.

- **Clinical pearl:** When asked which medication is "NOT likely" the cause, identify the drug without dopamine-antagonist activity at the tuberoinfundibular pathway — this is the expected answer in a hyperprolactinemia/galactorrhea scenario.
